Article Title: UP Creators Summit & Awards to celebrate the state's rising digital voices and creator economy in grand 2-day event
Article Text:
Times of India’s UP Creators Summit & Awards

Honouring the creators shaping a new Uttar Pradesh

Conversations driving the future of the creator economy

Preparing creators for the future

As India's creator economy continues to redefine entertainment, entrepreneurship and storytelling, Uttar Pradesh is emerging as one of the country's fastest-growing hubs for digital innovation. With increasing internet penetration, a thriving startup ecosystem and the rapid rise of creators from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, the state is playing a pivotal role in shaping India's digital future.Celebrating this transformation, the inaugural edition Times of India’s UP Creators Summit & Awards will bring together some of the state's most influential content creators, industry leaders, brands and digital innovators for a 2-day mega showcase of recognition, insightful conversations and future-focused learning.To be held on August 19 and 20 in Varanasi, the spiritual and cultural heart of Uttar Pradesh, the event will bring together the state’s rich heritage and its new-age digital voices, showcasing how creators are shaping the narrative of a new Uttar Pradesh. The first day, August 19, will feature insightful masterclasses, panel discussions and fireside chats, while August 20 will culminate in the grand UP Creators Awards, celebrating the state’s most impactful digital creators.At the heart of the event are the Creators Awards, which will honour creators who are making a meaningful impact across diverse genres, including education, technology, finance, food, travel, lifestyle, comedy, fashion, gaming, social impact and more. These creators are not only building communities online but are also amplifying local stories, inspiring millions and showcasing Uttar Pradesh's talent on the national and global stage. The awards celebrate creators who are redefining digital influence while contributing to the state's growing reputation as a powerhouse of innovation and creativity.Beyond the awards, the summit will serve as a platform for thought-provoking discussions on the opportunities and challenges shaping the creator ecosystem.Panel discussions will explore how the creator economy is expanding beyond metropolitan cities into Tier 2 and Tier 3 India, the growing influence of creators in rebranding Uttar Pradesh, and the role of digital storytellers in building the narrative of a new Uttar Pradesh. The event will also feature engaging fireside chats on themes such as "Storytellers of a New Bharat" and "Beyond Followers", examining how creators are moving beyond metrics to create meaningful impact, influence culture and build sustainable careers.As artificial intelligence reshapes the content landscape, the summit will host a dedicated AI Masterclass on future-proofing content creation. The session will provide practical insights into how creators can leverage AI-powered tools to enhance creativity, improve productivity and stay ahead in an increasingly competitive digital ecosystem.Bringing together creators, policymakers, industry experts and ecosystem enablers, the UP Creators Summit & Awards aims to celebrate the diverse voices driving India's digital revolution while highlighting Uttar Pradesh's emergence as one of the country's most exciting creator hubs. More than just an awards platform, the summit will spotlight the ideas, conversations and collaborations that are shaping the future of content creation in India.
Article Summary: Times of india’s up creators summit & awards will be held on august 19 and 20 in varanasi, the spiritual and cultural heart of uttar pradesh. The event will honour creators who are making a meaningful impact across diverse genres, including education, technology, finance, food, travel, lifestyle, comedy, fashion, gaming, social impact and more.

Article Title: From erotic fantasy to Indian identity, a famous Italian calendar finds a new story
Article Text:
Behind-the-scenes image featuring Avani Rai (left) during the Pirelli Calendar shoot in Delhi I Picture credit: Alessandro Scotti

One half of the 2027 Pirelli Calendar features Indian celebrities photographed by Norwegian photographer Sølve Sundsbø I Picture credit: Alessandro Scotti

In 1966, a photograph of a woman in underwear arrived at the Vatican. The fashion imagery might seem rather tame by today's standards, but it was enough to provoke an official complaint from the Holy See to an Italian tire company called Pirelli. The Milan-based tire manufacturer had just begun producing these exclusive, high-fashion calendars, simply called 'The Cal', as a trade gift for its top clients — the idea being to give VIPs something a cut above the cheap pin-up calendars that were standard fare in garages and tire shops at the time.But the condemnation had the opposite effect. Rather than suppressing the calendar, it generated enormous publicity, transforming a niche corporate giveaway into one of the world's most coveted cultural status symbols. Within a few years, the calendar became less a marketing gimmick and more an annual referendum on where European ideas of beauty, sex and provocation stood. Over the decades, figures from Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford and Kate Moss to Penélope Cruz, Serena Williams and Yoko Ono have been framed within its pages by some of the world's most influential photographers. But sixty-two years and a great many controversies later, the most recent edition of that same calendar is shot not on a Mediterranean beach or a Manhattan studio, but in the forts and villages of Rajasthan and the mean streets of Old Delhi, even featuring everyday barbers and artisans.The 2027 Pirelli Calendar is dedicated to India. For the first time, it features an all-India cast and is shot entirely in the country, built around the idea of Indian identity. So alongside glamorous portraits of celebrities like television host and author Padma Lakshmi, actress Aditi Rao Hydari, sitarist Anoushka Shankar and supermodel Bhavitha Mandava are some 200 ordinary Indians, from dancers and street artists to musicians and craftspeople.The project began as a collaboration between Norwegian photographer Sølve Sundsbø and Raghu Rai, modern India's most celebrated photojournalist known for chronicling the country's many faces and contradictions over several decades. Rai died in April shortly after the project began. His daughter, photographer Avani Rai, stepped in to complete it and in doing so changed its direction. What had been conceived as a studio shoot moved outdoors into the neighbourhoods her father spent his career documenting, from Kinari Bazar and Yamuna Ghat to the streets of Old Delhi.When asked how a project like the Pirelli Calendar sits alongside her reportage-driven practice, Avani, speaking to TOI, gently rejects the premise of the question. Genre, she argues, describes where a photograph ends up, not how it is made. What remains constant, whether in documentary work or a fashion commission, is the attempt to stay honest to what is in front of the camera. "Curiosity, presence and empathy are not specific to one genre of photography. The Pirelli Calendar asked me to bring those values into a different context. I wasn’t interested in making images that simply looked beautiful. I wanted them to feel alive. To hold the same emotional honesty that I search for in every photograph I make," says Avani whose mother, conservation architect Gurmeet Rai, also appears in the calendar.Even to this day, The Cal's physical copies are not sold publicly; Pirelli limits production to roughly 20,000 copies annually and they are sent as corporate gifts to monarchs, CEOs, prime ministers, top celebrities, fashion icons and the like.But why India? Sundsbø says it was a long-held ambition within Pirelli. His contribution came from a very different vantage point—that of an outsider conscious of his own limitations. "The fact that Avani and Raghu Rai’s images would be one half of the Calendar enabled me to concentrate on portraits. That's a smaller and more realistic task for a visitor than capturing the whole soul of a nation.I didn’t try to decide what “Indianness” should mean. Especially not as the guest that I am. I tried to cast people I admire, women who have inspirational talent," says Sundsbø.The edition also marks the first time Pirelli has commissioned two photographers to share a calendar. What makes the India edition notable is not simply that it swaps eroticism for cultural identity; the calendar has been moving in that direction for years. Rather, it is the first edition shaped by two intertwined perspectives: an outsider looking in and a daughter completing her father's final project in the streets he loved."I used to think inheritance was about continuing someone’s work. Now I think it’s about continuing their way of being in the world. The patience they lived with. The integrity they carried. The generosity with which they met people. Those are the things that survive," says Avani."Completing the calendar gave me a sense of continuity. It wasn’t about recreating him or holding onto the past. I understood that what he had really left me wasn’t an archive or even a body of work. It was a practice of being alive to the world," she adds.
Article Summary: The 2027 pirelli calendar is dedicated to india. For the first time, it features an all-india cast and is shot entirely in the country. The project began as a collaboration between norwegian photographer sølve sundsbø and raghu rai, modern india's most celebrated photojournalist.

Article Title: 5 indigenous small modular reactors targeted by 2033, Jitendra Singh tells LS
Article Text:
Union MoS Jitendra Singh speaks in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon session of Parliament

NEW DELHI: A key objective of the govt under the Nuclear Energy Mission is to develop and operationalise at least five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033, minister for department of atomic energy Jitendra Singh said in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday.Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is undertaking the design and development of indigenous SMR technologies, including the 220 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor (BSMR-200) and 55 MWe SMR-55 for power generation. BARC is also developing a high temperature gas cooled reactor (HTGCR) of up to 5 MW capacity, which can be coupled with a suitable thermochemical cycle for hydrogen production.Singh said India is steadily strengthening its indigenous nuclear energy ecosystem with a focus on advanced reactor technologies, SMRs, domestic manufacturing capabilities, private-sector participation and long-term utilisation of the country’s abundant thorium resources. The govt has adopted a two-pronged approach to accelerate nuclear capacity addition. This includes deployment of large indigenous reactors such as 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs) and advanced reactor designs at greenfield sites, alongside development and deployment of SMRs at brownfield locations, including retiring fossil-fuel-based power plants, captive plants for energy-intensive industries and off-grid applications in remote areas.The minister also highlighted continuing work of the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) in advancing the second stage of India’s nuclear power programme. IGCAR is pursuing multidisciplinary scientific research and advanced engineering development for sodium cooled fast breeder reactors and associated closed fuel-cycle facilities, technologies that remain a cornerstone of India’s long-term nuclear strategy.On thorium, Singh said India is pursuing its three-stage nuclear power programme, based on a closed fuel cycle, to optimise utilisation of its uranium resources and progressively harness its abundant thorium reserves. Thorium, being a fertile material, needs to be converted into fissile uranium-233 in a nuclear reactor before it can be used for energy generation.India has already undertaken sustained R&D towards thorium utilisation. Thorium Oxide (Thoria) pellets have been used in the initial cores of operating PHWRs, while Thoria-based fuels have also been irradiated in BARC research reactors. The irradiated Thoria pins have been reprocessed to obtain uranium-233, which has subsequently been fabricated as fuel for the KAMINI reactor at IGCAR, Kalpakkam. Singh said the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, 2025 has been enacted to enable wider participation of both public and private entities in the nuclear sector.
Article Summary: The govt under the nuclear energy mission is to develop and operationalise at least five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033. Bhabha atomic research centre (barc) is undertaking the design and development of indigenous smr technologies. The govt has adopted a two-pronged approach to accelerate nuclear capacity addition.

Article Title: Report: Aaron Rodgers caught secretly funding police cameras that spy on his own neighbours
Article Text:
All about Aaron Rodgers' wife.(Image via Getty Images)

Aaron Rodgers says he hates being watched, turns out he secretly funded a camera network to watch his neighbors

The guy who hates being watched, watching everyone else

The other side: Is this actually that deep?

Why the cameras themselves are the real controversy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Aaron Rodgers has spent years ranting about society's "sick" obsession with knowing his business. Turns out while he was busy protecting his own privacy, he was quietly bankrolling a surveillance system to keep tabs on everyone else's. A new report claims Rodgers secretly donated tens of thousands of dollars toward police license-plate cameras in his old New Jersey neighborhood, and used a shell company to hide that it was him. The irony has not been lost on anyone, least of all the internet.According to a report from the newsletter FOIAball, Rodgers dropped around $37,000 in 2024, back when he was still a Jet, on automatic license plate reader cameras for the Cedar Grove Police Department, near the mansion he was living in at the time.The donation was made through an LLC, allegedly so nobody in town would connect the dots back to him. At a city council meeting, the town manager thanked the mystery donor without naming names, calling it a "very generous donation" that gave police a useful new tool. Nobody in Cedar Grove had any idea their new surveillance upgrade came with a Hall of Fame quarterback attached, until now.This is a man who has said, on multiple occasions and on national television, that he can't stand people knowing anything about his life.He's called it a "sick society" obsessed with "entitlement to information."He's said his private life is going to stay private, full stop. And yet, behind the scenes, he was funding a system that tracks license plates of literally everyone who drives through his old neighborhood, all while making sure his own name stayed off the paperwork.To be fair to Rodgers, his paranoia isn't coming from nowhere. He's previously claimed paparazzi were flying drones over his New Jersey house, and he's talked openly about needing full-time security after Joe Burrow 's Ohio home got burglarized while Burrow was mid-game on Monday Night Football, an incident that also hit close to home given a similar break-in happened to Travis Kelce Rodgers even publicly urged other NFL players to use the league's security resources to protect their homes. So on some level, the guy funding cameras near his own house isn't shocking. What's shocking is that the cameras aren't pointed at his house, they're pointed at everyone else's, and he made sure his name wasn't attached.Not everyone's treating this as some grand hypocrisy. From LSU's side of the aisle- er, wrong story, but the same logic applies here - you could argue Rodgers did something genuinely public-minded: he paid for police equipment out of his own pocket, and the town got a free upgrade to its law enforcement toolkit.The town manager who thanked the anonymous donor didn't seem to have any complaints. If a rich guy wants to quietly pay for cop cameras instead of, say, another car, that's arguably more selfless than most celebrity spending. The read here really depends on how you feel about license plate readers in general.That's the bigger issue critics are raising, separate from Rodgers entirely: license plate readers are a lightning rod nationwide right now.Multiple towns have canceled or walked back their Flock-style camera contracts, the ACLU is running an active campaign against the company, and in some places, fed-up residents have gone as far as disguising themselves to destroy the cameras outright.The core complaint is that these systems track ordinary people's movements like where they go, when, how often, without consent or even awareness.One privacy policy expert framed the Rodgers situation as part of a bigger pattern of unelected, wealthy individuals essentially deciding how much surveillance an entire town has to live under, just because they can afford to write the check.Under that lens, it doesn't really matter whether Rodgers meant well, the point is that one person's money shouldn't get to set the privacy terms for everyone else in town.Rodgers hasn't addressed the report yet. Given how he's reacted to far smaller invasions of his own privacy, don't expect silence to last.
Article Summary: A new report claims rodgers secretly donated tens of thousands of dollars toward police license-plate cameras in his old new jersey neighborhood. The donation was made through an llc, allegedly so nobody in town would connect the dots back to him. At a city council meeting, the town manager thanked the mystery donor without naming names.

Article Title: Who is Gautam Rangarajan? Indian-origin strategist appointed to key role by UK PM Andy Burnham
Article Text:
Indian-origin strategist Gautam Rangarajan.

Who is Gautam Rangarajan ?

What will Gautam Rangarajan do at No. 10?

Burnham's government overhaul

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Indian-origin strategist and former BBC executive Gautam Rangarajan as an Expert Adviser on Structure and Process in a newly created role at 10 Downing Street.Rangarajan, who brings decades of experience in strategy, organisational transformation and media, is set to take up the position this week.Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive with more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting.Before his new government role, he spent more than 30 years at the BBC, beginning his career as a radio music producer and eventually rising to become the broadcaster's Group Director for Strategy and Performance.His experience includes developing strategy in rapidly changing markets, leading large-scale transformation initiatives and handling complex policy and financial negotiations.The exact details of Rangarajan's responsibilities are yet to be outlined. However, the UK PM's office said his appointment draws on his experience in corporate strategy and transformation.His role comes as Burnham undertakes a broader restructuring of the machinery of government, including the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.Rangarajan is expected to play a role in the planned transformation at the heart of the British government.Away from strategy and public service, Rangarajan also has a creative side. He describes himself as a professional choral singer and music producer, alongside his work in corporate strategy and organisational transformation.The appointment comes as Burnham reshapes his government following his recent rise to the role of Labour Party leader and Prime Minister.His administration has announced structural changes, including the launch of No. 10 North in Manchester and the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.While the full scope of Rangarajan's new role remains unclear, his appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox: "I think the scariest person in the world is the person with…" - a lesson on humour, perspective and facing hard times with lightness
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox (AP photo)

Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox

"I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor"

Where this quote actually comes from

Why humour matters most during genuinely difficult stretches

How humour actually helps people manage stress

Why laughing at your own mistakes actually matters

Why humour can genuinely strengthen relationships

Michael J. Fox's own perspective on adversity

Why humour is not the same thing as avoiding a real problem

Why being naturally serious is not actually a flaw

Other memorable quotes by Michael J. Fox

"One's dignity may be assaulted, vandalized and cruelly mocked, but it can never be taken away unless it is surrendered."

"I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection."

"Family is not an important thing. It's everything."

"Acceptance doesn't mean resignation; it means understanding that something is what it is and that there's got to be a way through it."

Why people still find meaning in this quote

Humour can genuinely change how a difficult moment actually feels. A stressful situation seems lighter once someone finds a reason to laugh, and a serious problem often becomes easier to approach once it can be seen from another angle. It can create a little distance from fear, frustration and uncertainty, even when the circumstances themselves have not changed. Michael J. Fox , the actor and Parkinson's disease advocate, put a striking twist on that idea. "I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor," he said. Not being able to laugh, in his framing, is not simply a personality quirk. It genuinely limits how someone can respond to life, and coming from someone who has lived with a serious, lifelong illness for decades, the line carries a good deal more weight than a passing joke.This line comes from an interview Fox gave to journalist Amy Wallace, published on Reader's Digest's website. Fox is not really suggesting that a humourless person is dangerous in any literal sense. He is pointing at the seriousness that tends to surround someone who cannot laugh at themselves, cannot recognise irony, and cannot find any lightness in a genuinely difficult moment. Humour creates real distance from a problem.It lets someone acknowledge that something is hard without letting it completely take over.Life inevitably brings disappointment, uncertainty and real stress. Humour cannot solve every problem on its own, but it can genuinely change how someone responds to one. Being able to laugh during a hard period offers a small emotional break, and it can help people communicate when a direct, serious conversation feels too uncomfortable to actually have. None of this means every situation deserves to be treated as a joke. Humour and genuine seriousness can exist side by side.Stress tends to narrow someone's attention down entirely onto the immediate problem in front of them. A moment of real laughter can interrupt that cycle. Research into humour and stress has suggested that positive humour can genuinely influence mood and help people cope with stressful experiences, and laughter itself is linked to physiological changes, including a release of muscle tension. None of this should be overstated. Humour is never a substitute for professional help or a practical solution when someone faces a genuinely serious problem. As an everyday coping tool, though, it can offer a genuinely useful shift in perspective.One of the most valuable forms of humour is simply being able to laugh at your own missteps. Nobody gets everything right. People mispronounce words, misjudge situations and occasionally embarrass themselves, and someone who can acknowledge a mistake without being consumed by embarrassment tends to find it easier to actually learn from it. Self-directed humour also tends to make social interactions considerably more comfortable, since it signals that a person does not expect flawless perfection from either themselves or anyone else around them.Shared laughter helps people form real connections. Friends, colleagues and family members often use humour to build a sense of familiarity and trust, and a well-placed joke can break tension that a serious conversation might struggle to shift on its own. There is an important line here worth being clear about, between humour that actually brings people together and humour that humiliates someone else. Jokes built on cruelty or prejudice tend to damage relationships rather than genuinely strengthen them, and the most constructive kind of humour has never really needed anyone else to get hurt.Fox became one of the most recognisable actors of his generation through films and television, including Back to the Future and Family Ties. In 1991, at the age of 29, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. He later made the diagnosis public and became a prominent advocate for Parkinson's research through the Michael J. Fox Foundation. His public approach to living with the condition has consistently included honesty, genuine optimism and humour, which gives his comments about laughter an extra dimension. His point was never that difficult experiences are inherently funny. It is that holding onto a sense of humour can help someone preserve real perspective while actually facing a genuine challenge.There is a meaningful difference between using humour to cope with something difficult and using it to avoid actually dealing with it at all. Some problems genuinely require serious attention and real action, and nobody can simply laugh away financial difficulty, illness or grief. What humour can offer instead is a small amount of emotional breathing space while someone continues addressing the actual underlying issue, which is really the whole distinction worth holding onto here.Fox's quote is deliberately provocative, and it should not be read as suggesting that serious people are inherently unpleasant. Some people naturally have quieter personalities, or simply express humour in a different way. The broader lesson is really about flexibility rather than personality type. Someone who can be genuinely serious when it matters, while still finding moments of humour elsewhere, tends to have more ways of responding to life's challenges than someone who treats every single situation with exactly the same level of weight.Humour is easy to underrate, since it can look insignificant next to more obviously serious qualities like intelligence or discipline. Even so, the ability to laugh genuinely shapes how people communicate, handle their own mistakes and respond to real difficulty. Fox's quote offers a deliberately provocative reminder that life does not always need to be approached with complete seriousness. There will be moments when humour is genuinely inappropriate, and problems that cannot be laughed away at all. In between those moments, though, holding onto a sense of humour tends to keep people connected, flexible and hopeful, which is really the whole point behind the line.
Article Summary: "i think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor" michael j. Fox, actor and parkinson's disease advocate. Not being able to laugh is not simply a personality quirk. It genuinely limits how someone can respond to life. Actor michael j. Fox was diagnosed with parkinson's disease in 1991.

Article Title: It's one year to Intel becoming a 'US government company', what has this meant for the chip giant
Article Text:
What government ownership means for Intel: Some good and some not-so-good things

The US government became the largest single shareholder in Intel on August 22, 2025, after announcing an $8.9 billion agreement to acquire a 9.9% equity stake (433.3 million shares) in the company. It's been almost a year since then. In what can be called as an unprecedented shift in the US industrial policy, the federal government acquired an approximate 10% equity stake in Intel Corporation, instantly becoming the semiconductor giant’s largest single shareholder.The transaction is part of a broader, sweeping initiative in which Washington is taking equity positions in 30 publicly traded companies spanning key economic sectors. By taking a direct ownership position in Intel—a flagship U.S. chipmaker with a market capitalization of approximately $491.9 billion—the government is signaling a fundamentally new approach to supporting and securing critical national technology infrastructure. Intel forms a key piece in the administration’s effort to restore the U.S.’s domestic manufacturing capacity. Earlier this year, the US President Donald Trump said that he should have asked for a bigger stake in Intel given its newfound success.“I said, ‘Give the country 10% ownership for free in Intel,’” Trump told Fortune Magazine in a May interview. “(Tan) said, ‘You have a deal.’ I said, ‘S—, I should have asked for more.’”The move marked a transformative moment for Intel as it works to execute a turnaround focused on next-generation AI architecture and contract foundry services. As the company competes against global heavyweights like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) and Nvidia, a backed-by-Washington status could serve as a powerful differentiator.For government agencies and defense contractors with sensitive computing workloads, a federally backed domestic supplier offers crucial supply-chain security and geopolitical reliability. The government's backing strengthens Intel’s core narrative: Positioning itself as a trusted, long-term provider of critical compute infrastructure where supply chain resilience is paramount.However, the unprecedented ownership structure has immediately raised concerns among Wall Street analysts and corporate governance experts. Government involvement introduces novel questions regarding potential political interference, regulatory conflicts of interest, and capital allocation.Intel is already navigating significant execution risks, including massive capital expenditure plans and a recent $20 billion share offering. Investors worry that sovereign ownership could slow down decision-making, entangle the company in bureaucracy, or force policy-driven trade-offs at the expense of shareholder returns.Industry observers note that the federal intervention in Intel could set a wide-reaching precedent. As governments worldwide rush to secure domestic hardware capacity for artificial intelligence, Washington's move may herald a permanent shift toward state-backed corporate partnerships across the broader AI infrastructure landscape.
Article Summary: The us government became the largest single shareholder in intel on august 22, 2025. The government is signaling a fundamentally new approach to supporting and securing critical national technology infrastructure. The move marked a transformative moment for intel as it works to execute a turnaround focused on next-generation ai architecture.

Article Title: Gates Foundation donates $540 million grant to University of Washington for research on…
Article Text:
Gates Foundation makes one of its biggest investments in health research

Gates Foundation's $540 million grant to expand health research

Long partnership between Gates Foundation and IHME

The Gates Foundation has announced a $540 million grant to the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington, marking one of its biggest investments in health research. As reported by Fortune, the 10-year funding will help expand global health data and research used by governments and policymakers to respond to disease outbreaks and improve healthcare. The donations come as the US government continues to reduce funding for scientific research, public health, education and other programmes, the report says, adding that the billionaire philanthropy is increasingly filling gaps left by federal funding cuts in the US.Gates Foundation's $540 million grant will allow IHME to expand its Global Burden of Disease study, which measures diseases, injuries and health risks across the world. According to the foundation, the project will increase its coverage from about 925 locations to nearly 5,000, giving governments and researchers more detailed local health data to support policy decisions.“Reliable and independent evidence can mean the difference between reacting to a health crisis after it has taken hold and acting early enough to change its course,” said Dr.Christopher J.L. Murray, IHME director and professor of health metrics sciences.“This investment will allow us to provide high-quality evidence at a much more local level and help leaders understand not only where health is improving or worsening, but which decisions can make the greatest difference for people,” he added.The latest funding builds on a long relationship between the Gates Foundation and IHME. The foundation provided the original funding to establish the research institute at the University of Washington in 2007. Since then, IHME has become one of the world's leading sources of public health data and disease research.Gates Foundation to shut down operations by 2045Gates Foundation has previously announced plans to wind down operations by 2045 and significantly increase its charitable spending over the next two decades. Earlier this year, the foundation said it would distribute $9 billion in 2026 while reducing its workforce as part of preparations for its planned closure. Bill Gates has also pledged to give away almost all of his wealth, with the foundation planning to spend more than $200 billion by 2045.
Article Summary: Gates foundation makes one of its biggest investments in health research. 10-year funding will help expand global health data and research. Donations come as us government continues to reduce funding for scientific research, public health, education and other programmes.

Article Title: Can I use soapy water to clean TV screen? Here’s what you should know
Article Text:
Tips to to clean TV screen safely (AI-generated image)

How to clean TV screen safely with soap

Dip a clean microfiber cloth into the solution

Wring it out thoroughly so it is only slightly damp.

Wipe the screen gently using light, circular motions without pressing hard.

Once clean, use a dry microfiber cloth to remove any remaining moisture.

Things that you should never use to clean your TV screen

Never use glass cleaner on a TV screen

Avoid paper towels

Don't use household cleaning sprays

Skip rubbing alcohol and harsh chemicals

Never spray water directly on the screen

Don't use rough cloths or old rags

Avoid excessive pressure while cleaning

Avoid baby wipes or wet wipes

Don't use abrasive sponges or scrubbers

Cleaning a TV screen looks like a simple job, but the wrong product or tool can scratch the display, strip its protective coating, or cause permanent damage. Modern LED, OLED, QLED and Mini-LED televisions come with delicate anti-glare and anti-reflective coatings that need careful handling. One question often asked is whether one can use soapy water to clean a TV screen? The short answer is: not directly. While a small amount of diluted soapy water may be recommended for stubborn stains, using too much soap, spraying liquid directly on the display, can damage the screen's protective coating or allow moisture to seep inside the TV.If you need to remove stubborn fingerprints or greasy marks, use only a very small amount of mild dish soap mixed with distilled water.Note: Avoid using strong detergents or excess soap, as they can damage the screen's protective coating.Experts say only approved cleaning methods should be used, and have flagged several household items that people commonly reach for by mistake. Here's a look at what to avoid when cleaning your TV screen, and why.Most glass cleaners contain ammonia, alcohol or other harsh chemicals that can damage the protective coating on modern displays.These products may work fine on windows or mirrors, but on a TV screen they can leave streaks and permanently alter its finish.Paper towels may feel soft, but they contain wood fibres that can scratch the screen over time. Addiitnally, they can also leave lint behind, making the display look dirtier after cleaning.Multi-purpose cleaners, kitchen cleaners and disinfectant sprays are not designed for electronics. Spraying them directly on the TV can damage its screen and may allow liquid to seep into the edges of the screen.Strong cleaning agents such as rubbing alcohol, acetone, bleach or ammonia-based products can strip away the anti-reflective coating found on many modern televisions. Once damaged, the coating cannot be restored.Water sprayed onto a display can run down and seep into the TV through its edges or vents, raising the risk of internal damage. If moisture is needed, a lightly dampened microfiber cloth is the safer route.Old T-shirts, towels, tissues and rough fabric can carry dirt or coarse fibres that scratch the display. A clean microfiber cloth remains the safest choice for wiping away dust and fingerprints.Pressing hard on the screen can damage the display panel, especially on OLED and LED TVs. Use light, gentle strokes instead of scrubbing stubborn marks.Wet wipes or for that matter baby wipes contain cleaning chemicals, fragrances or moisturisers that are not safe for TV screens. Using wet wipes on screen can leave residue and may damage the coating over time.Kitchen sponges, scouring pads or abrasive cleaning tools can permanently scratch the TV screen, even with gentle use. These products should never be used on electronic displays.
Article Summary: Cleaning a tv screen looks like a simple job, but the wrong product or tool can scratch the display, strip its protective coating, or cause permanent damage. Modern led, oled, qled and mini-led televisions come with delicate anti-glare and anti-reflective coatings that need careful handling.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.
